To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a new technique for labeling human mesenchymal stromal cells (hMSC) with magnetic particles that can be detected by magnetic resonance imaging and fluorescent microscopy, which can be used for tracking hMSC after grafting in a model of stroke.
clinical‐grade h MSCs can be efficiently labeled with M‐SPIO particles without affecting their phenotype and can be tracked in vivo by MRI and fluorescence microscopy in a rat model after stroke.

we developed a method of labeling hMSCs with M‐SPIO that does not alter cell viability, differentiation, and phenotype, but may induce cell death and release of iron particles following grafting in a rodent stroke model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a new strategy of labeling hMSCs for in vivo MRI that is simple and efficient and does not alter cell viability and/or phenotype.
the development of an efficient, noninvasive, and safe MRI method for the detection of hMSCs in vivo following graft.
the use of a novel labeling method for hMSCs that is efficient, safe, and noninvasive for both in vitro and in vivo MRI tracking of hMSCs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
M‐SPIO‐based labeling of clinical‐grade h MSCs can be performed without impacting cell phenotype or in vitro differentiation.
M‐SPIO‐labeled hMSCs may be useful in vivo for MRI tracking in the early stages following grafting, but that the long‐term effects of M‐SPIO on hMSCs should be further investigated.
M‐SPIO‐labeled clinical‐grade h‐MSCs can be detected in vivo by MRI and histology.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MRI and fluorescent labeling of hMSCs using M‐SPIO can be used for in vivo cell tracking in a rat model without impacting their phenotype.
M‐SPIO is a safe, efficient, and versatile label for hMSC imaging in vivo, but that it should be used with caution in clinical applications.
M‐SPIO is a good candidate for hMSCs labeling, but the in vivo stability of the label should be further investigated.
The main takeaway from our work is that
M‐SPIO can be used to label hMSCs without altering their properties.
M‐SPIO‐labeling of hMSCs does not induce any cell damage and can be used for in vivo MRI tracking.
M‐SPIO‐labeled hMSCs can be used for both MRI tracking of cells in vivo after stroke and for fluorescent microscopy of cell distribution.
